revision_notes: The initial 0/Unknown score had no source and was unresearched rather than a confirmed absence of data, so this was moved to the full verification path. Current (2025/26) LEC/LEWA-approved tariffs show a domestic (standard) rate of M2.08/kWh and a lifeline rate of M0.93/kWh for qualifying low-consumption users (lewa.org.ls; lndc.org.ls, effective 1 April 2025). World Bank GNI per capita (Atlas method) for Lesotho was US$1,180 in 2024 (~M1,790-1,800/month at the ~M18.2:US$1 loti/rand rate prevailing through 2025). Applying these tariffs to typical residential consumption (roughly 30 kWh at lifeline rate plus additional usage up to an average ~90 kWh/month, per World Bank rural electrification analysis) yields a monthly bill of roughly M150-190, i.e. approximately 8-10% of monthly GNI per capita — placing Lesotho in the 'Expensive (6-10%)' band (code 2). A dedicated 2016/17 World Bank SREP assessment separately found that 50 kWh of monthly consumption cost at least 10% of monthly income for nearly half of Lesotho households, and tariffs have risen further since (a 32% increase in 2020, a further 9.6% increase in April 2025) while GNI per capita has been broadly flat, suggesting affordability may be worse (potentially 'Very Expensive', code 1) for lower-income households specifically. No single, current, primary source computes this ratio directly for Lesotho as a national figure, so this recalculation rests on combining tariff, exchange-rate and GNI data across sources rather than one authoritative computed statistic — flagging for human review rather than asserting a precise final code.
revised_comments: Lesotho's grid electricity is moderately to highly expensive relative to income. The Lesotho Electricity and Water Authority (LEWA) approved tariffs effective April 2025 set a domestic (standard) rate of M2.08/kWh and a discounted lifeline rate of M0.93/kWh for qualifying low-consumption households, alongside separate general-purpose, commercial and industrial rates. With GNI per capita around US$1,180 (2024, World Bank Atlas method), a typical residential consumption pattern (a base lifeline allowance plus additional consumption at the standard rate) implies a monthly electricity bill equivalent to roughly 8-10% of monthly income, and poorer households consuming even modest amounts (around 50 kWh/month) have historically faced bills exceeding 10% of monthly income. Given Lesotho's high poverty rate (over half the population) and tariffs that have risen faster than incomes in recent years, electricity affordability remains a material barrier to ICT adoption and to the viability of data infrastructure for a significant share of the population.
